builderInsights.title: Andrej Karpathy
builderInsights.suggestedTitle: LLMは単なる高速なソフトウェアではない。新しいソフトウェアである
builderInsights.suggestedSummary: 彼が言う本当の変化は、コーディングの高速化ではない。LLMは、以前はほぼ不可能だったものを動かせる。たとえば、従来のコードなしで動くimage-in/image-outアプリ、Markdownで書かれたインストール手順、雑然とした非構造データの上に成り立つknowledge baseだ。さらに彼は、LLMがぎこちなさを残すのは、labsが学習させる対象が経済性と検証可能性に左右されるからだと主張する。そのため、巨大なcodebaseを一瞬でrefactorできる一方で、次の瞬間にはとんでもない助言も出す。より大きな賭けは、agent-nativeな経済圏だ。そこでは、製品は人間だけでなくモデルにとっても読み取りやすいように作られる。

tweets.text: This is the the quote I've been citing a lot recently. https://t.co/H4Fyxrv2pv

Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights:

The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons:

1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing.
2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM".  The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc.
3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc.

I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3).

The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to...

Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors.

builderInsights.title: Aaron Levie
builderInsights.suggestedTitle: agentがUIを食い尽くし、APIがproductになる
builderInsights.suggestedSummary: 彼の主張は、softwareはheadlessである必要があるというものだ。agentはUIをクリックして回るのではなく、APIに直接話しかけるからだ。Boxでの見立てでは、今後も人はseatを買う。ただし、そのseatにはbundled API usageが必要になる。さらに、agent-onlyの仕事が増えるほど、softwareはconsumption pricingとoutcome-based APIへ向かう。

tweets.text:
As agents become the biggest users of software, then all software has to be available in a headless fashion. Agents won’t be using your UI, they’ll be talking to your APIs.

So the question becomes what is the business model of software and this headless approach in the future?

Here are a few thoughts on how everything plays out based on what we’re seeing and doing at Box, but also conversation with other platforms.

1) Seats don’t go away for *people*. Seats are still a convenient and efficient way to have a customer use technology predictably for a set of users within a baseline set of usage. The key, though, is that when the customer pays for a seat, it has to come with a set of usage of APIs on behalf of that user that the agent can use on their behalf. 

The user will need to be able to interact with their data and the underlying tool via any agent they work with, and an embedded amount of usage will come with the seat. I would imagine most software -Box included- will enable seats to work with their data at a relatively high volume via systems like ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot, Perplexity, Factory, Cogniton, et al. quite seamlessly. If you don’t do this, you’re DOA.

2) Agents may have “seats” if they are doing stateful work in the system, but they will be priced very differently than people. Seats (or the equivalent) can make sense when you have an agent that has its own workspace, stores its own data, needs a different set of permissions compared to the user, and so on. 

If a company wants this agent to be around for long period of time, that may very well look like another “user” in the system. Openclaw-style agents highlight what this future could look like. 

The only issue on pricing here is that one customer could decide to do all their work in 1 agent, and another might split it into 1,000 agents. So pricing like a human seat is nearly impossible and impractical; each company will have a different approach for this as it gets tricky perfectly trying to capture all the value within an agent seat.

3) The dominant pricing for headless use that goes above the seat allotment, or when an agent is firmly acting on their own, will be a consumption model. Many enterprises software platforms have previously operated like this with PaaS options, and agents will look like another machine user of their system. 

In some cases the APIs might get priced just as they did previously, but in other cases there may need to be new types of APIs that represent the work an agent would do in one go -more akin to an outcome- instead of a series of API calls. This is especially germane when the headless software also has an agentic use-case embedded within in, such as orchestrating the process within their own system via AI.

Overall the growth of this usage pattern is effectively unbounded as the use-cases for agents operating on data in these systems will dramatically exceed what people do with their data and tools today. Every platform that goes headless (which will be anyone that wants to take advantage of agents) will need to adopt a model like this. Some may fight it initially but it’s an inevitably as there will always be more and more agents outside your platform than people.

Overall, there’s a lot of really interesting changes left to come in software due to headless use of these systems. Early days.

no opinion is opinionated

people treat "opinionated" and "general purpose" as opposites. they're not.

the moment you decide what concepts exist, what's visible, what composes, what extends, what hides – you've already expressed a worldview. "no opinion" is itself a strong one.

building for universality means saying something very specific: core concepts should be few, durable, and flexible. users shouldn't be trapped in rigid workflows. abstraction matters more than surface specialization. the system should fold into many shapes without breaking its underlying logic.

this is also why pure customer-centricity falls short. user feedback tells you where friction is. it rarely tells you what the underlying system should be. if you only follow direct user demand, you converge on local maxima – fragmented features, narrow tools, products shaped around current habits rather than enduring concepts.

that gap is where design lives. the work of simplifying reality below the level that's immediately obvious.

great systems don't start by multiplying products. they start by reducing concepts to their essence – until the primitives become clear. then you build paths for each concept to extend, combine, fold into others. the packaging can vary. the essence shouldn't.

this is what lets a system serve beginners without capping experts. serve one domain without being trapped by it.

flexibility isn't the absence of opinion. it's the result of a strong opinion held in cohesion – not about one ideal workflow, but about which concepts are fundamental, which abstractions should endure, which degrees of freedom matter.

simple at the core. open at the edges. that's the ultimate opinion.

podcastHighlights.title: Demis HassabisがDeepMind、AlphaFold、そしてAGIへの最後の追い込みを築くまで
podcastHighlights.suggestedTitle: Demis Hassabis: まずAIを道具として作り、そこから科学を書き換える
podcastHighlights.suggestedSummary:
**要点:** HassabisはAGIを長期戦として捉えている。まず強力な道具を作る。そしてそれを使って、科学、医療、そして理解そのものを加速させる。

- 彼はAIに偶然たどり着いたのではない。10代のころから計画していた。ゲーム、神経科学、スタートアップを、DeepMindへ向かう踏み石として使った。
- 彼の最大のスタートアップ教訓は、容赦なく実践的だ。「時代の5年先を行け。50年先を行くな」というものだ。
- AlphaFoldは、AIが何年分ものwet-lab作業を、ほぼin-silicoの探索に圧縮できる証拠だと彼は見ている。生物学は、シミュレーター駆動の科学になりつつある。

DeepMindとIsomorphic Labsの背後にいる神経科学者兼創業者、Demis Hassabisは、煽るタイプというより、規律ある戦略家に見える。彼によれば、キャリアを貫く一本線は最初からAIだった。ゲームは資金調達の手段であり、神経科学は着想の源であり、DeepMindは本当の使命のための器だった。Theme Parkでの初期の成功は、人々が知的なシステムとの対話を好むことを示した。Republicの野心的な失敗は、ビジョンと同じくらいタイミングが重要だと教えた。

彼の哲学は、驚くほど感傷がない。DeepMindの当初の使命は「第一段階、知能を解く。第二段階、それを使って他のすべてを解く」だった。彼が最も熱を入れているのは、その第二段階だ。科学のためのAI。とくに生物学、気象、そして最終的にはシミュレーションを通じた社会システムである。彼は、生物学こそmachine learningに最適な領域だと主張する。複雑で、創発的で、人間の頭では抱えきれない弱いシグナルに満ちているからだ。目標は、探索の99%をcomputerにやらせ、labは検証に残すことだ。

AGIについても、彼の考えは神秘的ではなく具体的だ。まず「信じられないほど知的で、有用で、精密なtool」を作る。そして次のRubiconを越える。しかも彼は、依然として大きく哲学的なことも考えている。「私は、情報こそが最も根本的だと思っている」

blogUpdates.title: デスクトップ版 Claude Code を並列 agent 向けに再設計
blogUpdates.suggestedTitle: Claude Code のデスクトップ版が並列セッションと内蔵ツールを追加
blogUpdates.suggestedSummary:
**要点:** 再設計された Claude Code のデスクトップアプリが利用可能になった。新しいサイドバー、ドラッグ＆ドロップのワークスペースレイアウト、統合された terminal とファイルエディタ、さらに高速なレビュー機能を備え、並列 agent ワークフロー向けに作られている。

**数値:**
- Claude Code ユーザー向けに、**Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise** プランで現在利用可能。**Claude API** 経由でも使える。
- **SSH support** は **Mac** と **Linux** にも拡張された。
- インターフェースモードは 3 種類。**Verbose, Normal, Summary**。

**意味するところ:** 今回のアップデートで、Claude Code はより orchestration hub に近づいた。複数のセッションを repo をまたいで走らせられる。メインのスレッドを汚さずに side chat に分岐できる。work が merge されたり close されたりしても、全体を整理したまま保てる。Claude はこのアプリを「**how agentic coding actually feels now: many things in flight, and you in the orchestrator seat**」のために作ったとしている。builder はアプリを離れずに diff を review し、test を実行し、file を edit し、HTML/PDF を preview できる。plugin の互換性と remote-session support により、既存の workflow にもそのままなじむ。実用上のポイントは、context switching が減り、iteration が速くなり、terminal と editor を行き来する手間の一部を desktop 体験で置き換えられることだ。
